title: COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions - Carbon Brief
gist: At COP31 in Antalya, UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband defended UK climate leadership despite the Jackdaw gas approval, framed electrification as an energy-security answer for fossil-fuel importers, backed the 35x35 electrification pledge (formally endorsed hours later), and argued coalitions of the willing within the COP and MDB reform under the UK's 2027 G20 presidency are the main levers for progress.

themes.theme: UK climate credibility vs Jackdaw and EV rollback

insights.claim: UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband argued at COP31 that the UK's approval of the Jackdaw gas field and rumoured rollback of EV targets have not dented its standing as a climate leader, citing its world-leading clean power 2030 target and legislation for no new oil and gas licences.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: UK policy signals mix new gas approval with a ban on new licences; investors in North Sea and UK EV supply chains face policy ambiguity.
insights.quote: People don’t see us as rolling back, and I think what people see is a government that is driving the agenda on electrification and clean power.
insights.locator: How, in your experience at COP31

insights.claim: Ed Miliband said the UK will 'go all out' to meet its 2030 NDC of cutting emissions 68% below 1990 levels but conceded the target is stretching and blamed a difficult inheritance from the previous government in 2024.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Admission that the 68% target is stretching hints at delivery risk and possible further policy push (or slippage) in UK decarbonisation.
insights.quote: Obviously, it’s stretching. We inherited, from 2024, a difficult situation from the previous government
insights.locator: Are you confident that the UK

insights.claim: Ed Miliband acknowledged the UK lacks a national climate education programme despite UNFCCC and Paris commitments, pointing instead to the annual climate and nature statement he started in 2025 and Mary Creagh repeated in 2026.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Public-information gaps amid misinformation are a soft risk to political durability of UK net-zero policy.
insights.quote: We need to do more. You’re completely right.
insights.locator: We need to do more. You’re

insights.claim: Ed Miliband frames climate as a national security issue, arguing that politicians not serious about climate are not serious about national security.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Reframing climate as security can protect clean-energy budgets from fiscal cuts and broaden political support, favouring defence-adjacent energy spending.
insights.quote: if you’re serious about national security, you need to be serious about climate
insights.locator: And what I’m trying to do here

insights.claim: Ed Miliband argued that the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the Iran war show security cannot be built on fossil fuels, since fossil-fuel importers covering 75% of the world's population, including the UK, are price takers exposed to price shocks.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Oil and gas price volatility from geopolitical conflict is the core political driver for importer-country electrification spending.
insights.quote: for fossil-fuel importers, covering 75% of the world’s population [including the UK], we are price takers

insights.claim: Ed Miliband said even a massive fossil-fuel producer like America is affected by higher prices, so clean electrification is the answer to the 'fossil-fuel rollercoaster' and cost-of-living pressures.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Positions electrification as an affordability play, not only a climate one, supporting demand for grids, heat pumps and EVs.

insights.claim: The UK government confirmed its endorsement of the Turkish COP31 presidency's 35x35 electrification pledge three hours after Ed Miliband told Carbon Brief the UK supports it while calling it stretching for the UK.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: A UK commitment to accelerate electrification signals policy tailwinds for grid, storage and electric heat/transport suppliers.
insights.quote: It’s stretching for the UK, but we think it’s the right thing to do.

insights.claim: Electrification is described as a big focus of the Turkish COP31 presidency in Antalya, alongside events on forests, green industrial policy, methane and climate security.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Electrification is the headline industrial theme of COP31, likely shaping coalition pledges and capital flows.

themes.theme: Defending the COP and coalitions of the willing

insights.claim: Ed Miliband defended the COP institution by noting the world was heading for 4C at the acrimonious 2009 Copenhagen COP but is now heading for about 2.5-2.6C according to the latest UNEP emissions gap report, which he credits to multilateralism.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Projected warming of about 2.6C still implies large adaptation and physical-risk costs, even as progress continues.
insights.quote: We were heading for a 4C world back then. Now, we’re heading for a 2.5C, 2.6C world
insights.locator: One, if you look at the sweep

insights.claim: Ed Miliband rejected the narrative that the COP process has run its course, arguing the COP is where coalitions of the willing form, so mini-coalitions complement rather than replace it.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Expect more action via plurilateral coalitions (methane, forests, electrification) than via consensus COP text.
insights.quote: it’s not simply a talking shop. I think it is also a place where action happens
insights.locator: It’s become part of the narrative

insights.claim: Ed Miliband said countries blocking consensus mean Brazil's fossil-fuel roadmap may not enter the formal COP decision, but a coalition of 80 or more countries formed last year is driving it forward and individual countries should build on it.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Fossil-fuel phase-down will advance unevenly through voluntary coalitions, not binding global text, limiting near-term hit to producers.
insights.quote: there are countries that are obstacles to the fossil-fuel roadmap
insights.locator: I think what’s interesting about this

themes.theme: Climate finance via MDB reform and UK G20

insights.claim: Facing fiscal pressure in developed countries, Ed Miliband said multilateral development bank reform to leverage MDB balance sheets is the biggest lever, potentially unlocking hundreds of billions of dollars for developing countries' resilience and debt relief.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Balance-sheet stretching at MDBs is the substitute for shrinking bilateral aid, a key channel for emerging-market climate investment.
insights.quote: the MDBs could do more to leverage their balance sheets
insights.locator: There’s lots of evidence out there

insights.claim: Ed Miliband said the UK will use its 2027 G20 presidency to convene MDBs, highlight best practice and push laggards, with climate resilience and debt development central to the agenda.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: 2027 G20 could be a catalyst for MDB capital-adequacy changes and emerging-market debt initiatives.
insights.locator: And, you know, one of the things

insights.claim: Ed Miliband said a key COP31 outcome he seeks is getting methane onto the formal COP agenda via a coalition of the willing, calling it an important short-term lever for curbing temperature rise.
insights.speaker: Simon Evans
insights.so_what: Methane focus raises regulatory and abatement exposure for oil, gas and agriculture, and demand for leak-detection technology.
